headline: US midterms tomorrow, oil slides on Iran diplomacy hopes, and Citi cuts lithium forecasts — a rough session across the board but no reason to panic.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO slipped last night as broader NASDAQ sold off sharply (-2.86%). The stock is also carrying some uncertainty heading into November — earnings are due, a union ballot is underway, and investors are still asking the GTA VI question. Nothing structural has changed; this is market noise plus pre-earnings jitters.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft actually beat on both earnings and revenue in its latest quarterly report — so the dip last night is frustrating but not company-specific. The broader tech sell-off dragged it down with everything else. The underlying result was solid, with cloud acceleration continuing. Long-term story is intact.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Alphabet fell last night after a notable milestone: Google Search dropped below 50% of Alphabet's total revenue for the first time. Markets are spooked by what that means for its core business, even though it reflects growing cloud and AI revenue streams. The $500B market cap drop over recent sessions reflects genuine re-rating anxiety — worth watching but not a sell signal for a long-term holder.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS slipped again today after Citi cut its lithium price forecasts on worsening battery demand outlook. Australian lithium stocks broadly sold off. Pilbara is trying to ride out the slump through cost control, but the macro headwind remains real. This is a long-term turnaround story — patience required.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF dipped modestly today, reflecting the broader tech weakness flowing through from Wall Street's rough night. Morgan Stanley also warned of a potential further 15% decline in semiconductor ETFs, which are a core part of GXAI's holdings. Short-term pressure; long-term AI thematic still has momentum.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: Slight dip in line with the broader ASX softness today. The ASX 200 fell 0.58% as global uncertainty around US midterms and the Iran situation weighed on sentiment. Nothing company-specific here — just a quiet, slightly down day for the whole market.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS nudged lower today tracking last night's weak US session. The NASDAQ fell nearly 3% and the S&P dropped 1.82%, so a 0.3% dip in the ASX-listed ETF is actually relatively contained. Still up 3.1% overall — the best performer in the portfolio by P&L percentage.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG edged slightly lower today alongside the broader market. Its diversified mix of Aussie and international shares means it absorbed the global wobble without too much drama. A very minor move — essentially flat.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was almost unchanged today — the most stable holding in the portfolio this session. Emerging markets have been relatively insulated from the US midterm and Iran noise. Steady as she goes.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Earnings due this month — hold ahead of the result
watch_today.detail: Take-Two has earnings coming up in November alongside a union ballot and ongoing GTA VI speculation. For a long-term holder, there's no reason to sell before the result — but be prepared for short-term volatility around the announcement. The long-term thesis (GTA VI is a potential blockbuster) hasn't changed. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Citi cuts lithium forecasts — headwinds building
watch_today.detail: Citi slashed lithium price forecasts today citing weaker-than-expected battery demand. Australian lithium stocks sold off broadly, and PLS is already down 61% from your cost base. The company is focusing on cost control to survive the downturn, but there's no near-term catalyst for a recovery. If you believe in the long-term EV story, hold — but this is a waiting game that could take another 12-18 months.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Search revenue milestone spooks markets — but cloud is growing
watch_today.detail: Google Search falling below 50% of Alphabet's revenue for the first time triggered a sharp re-rating last night. But analysts at Seeking Alpha note this is partly because cloud and AI revenue (via TPUs — custom AI chips) are accelerating. David Sacks called it a positive sign of diversification. The stock is down 9.5% from your cost base. Long-term holders should sit tight — the AI infrastructure story at Google is real.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Beat earnings but still sold off — don't read too much into it
watch_today.detail: Microsoft beat on both revenue and earnings in its FY27 Q1 result, with cloud acceleration continuing. Last night's 1.55% dip was purely macro — the whole NASDAQ sold off. This is one of the strongest-performing positions in the portfolio (+17.8% overall). Nothing to do here except hold with confidence.

watch_today.title: Oil falls 3.7% on Iran diplomacy signals — watch for flow-on effects
watch_today.detail: Crude oil dropped from $104 to $100 a barrel last night after Trump signalled he wants more time for diplomacy with Iran. This is a big move — oil had been rising on war fears. Cheaper oil is generally good for inflation (and therefore good for interest rates coming down), but it's worth watching whether the diplomatic signals hold. The Gulf region is still braced for potential escalation.

watch_today.title: RBA rate rise looming — Aussie housing and your spending power
watch_today.detail: Multiple headlines today point to the RBA preparing another interest rate rise, with the AFR suggesting rates could go well above 4.85%. NSW Premier Minns warned that another rise will see 'shops close that don't reopen.' Home borrowers are facing an estimated $6,000 annual hit. This affects discretionary spending broadly — and is a reason to keep an eye on any Aussie consumer-exposed holdings.

world.summary: The US midterm elections dominate global attention heading into Tuesday, with concerns about voter intimidation and potential challenges to results. Meanwhile, the US-Iran situation keeps oil markets on edge, even as diplomatic signals briefly calmed prices.

stories.title: US midterm elections: Democrats tipped for a 'blue wave' — or even a flood
stories.why_it_matters: Americans vote in midterm elections on Tuesday (US time), with polls and forecasters pointing to a significant Democrat gains — possibly enough for a 'blue flood' that would hand them control of the House and potentially the Senate. Trump made a final campaign push over the weekend. The result will reshape who controls Congress for the next two years and could directly affect US policy on AI regulation, trade, and the economy — all of which flow through to Australian investors with US holdings.

stories.title: Former security chiefs warn Trump could try to overturn midterm results
stories.why_it_matters: Former US national security officials are publicly warning that Trump may attempt to challenge or overturn midterm election results if the outcome goes against Republican candidates. Election officials across the country are also bracing for potential violence and intimidation at polling booths. A federal judge already rejected one Trump administration attempt to pause Alaska's Senate election. Political instability in the US — the world's largest economy — creates uncertainty for global markets, including Australian superannuation funds heavily exposed to US stocks.

stories.title: US-Iran war fears: Gulf braced for escalation as oil briefly spikes then retreats
stories.why_it_matters: Tensions between the US-Israel alliance and Iran remain extremely high, with Gulf states bracing for potential escalation. Iran has warned that any renewed war could outlast previous conflicts. Oil briefly surged on these fears before dropping more than 3% overnight after Trump signalled he wants more diplomatic time — bringing crude from $104 down to $100 a barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil passes, is at the centre of the risk. If conflict escalates, petrol prices globally — including at Australian bowsers — would spike sharply.

stories.title: World watches US midterms as 'Trumpism' wanes globally
stories.why_it_matters: International observers note that while Trumpism reshaped global politics, many allied countries are seeing right-wing populist movements lose momentum. The Japan Times points to shifting sentiment across Europe and Asia. The midterm results will be closely watched as a signal of whether the US is entering a new political phase — which has implications for alliances, trade deals, and the overall stability of the global economic order that Australia depends on.

stories.title: Argentina's Milei pitches a regulation-free AI haven
stories.why_it_matters: Argentina's President Javier Milei is actively marketing his country as a zero-regulation AI development hub, pitching to global tech companies looking to avoid the heavy AI rules being debated in the US and EU. It's a bold and unconventional play that reflects the global race to attract AI investment — and underscores how regulation (or the lack of it) is becoming a key competitive factor between nations. For investors in AI-exposed stocks, it's a signal that the regulatory landscape remains fragmented and unpredictable globally.

markets.summary: A rough night on Wall Street last night, with the NASDAQ dropping nearly 3% and the S&P falling 1.82% as investors grew cautious ahead of the US midterms and reacted to tech earnings. The ASX followed with a modest 0.58% decline today. Oil fell sharply on Iran diplomacy signals while gold edged up — a classic 'risk-off' pattern where investors move toward safety.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Modest dip today, following Wall Street's lead. Midterm uncertainty and RBA rate fears weighed on sentiment.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw broad selling ahead of the US midterms. Tech led the decline.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Tech took the biggest hit last night — nearly 3% down — as AI and growth stocks sold off broadly.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil fell sharply after Trump signalled more time for Iran diplomacy, easing immediate war fears.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold nudged higher as investors moved toward safe-haven assets amid political and geopolitical uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was almost flat — holding just above 70 US cents. RBA rate expectations and global risk sentiment keeping it rangebound.

politics.summary: The RBA rate rise drum is beating louder, with multiple warnings about the economic pain ahead for households and small businesses. On the political stage, Matt Canavan makes a move, and Gina Rinehart blasts the government over its energy agenda.

stories.title: RBA set to raise rates again — and the pain is real
stories.why_it_matters: NSW Premier Chris Minns warned today that another RBA interest rate hike — which looks increasingly likely — will cause 'shops to close that don't reopen.' The AFR reports home borrowers face a $6,000 annual hit from current rate settings, and analysis suggests rates could go well above 4.85%. The ABC outlined how the RBA's policy is effectively redistributing wealth from mortgage holders to savers. For everyday Australians with a home loan, the message is grim: more pain is coming, and house prices are already sliding.

stories.title: Westpac posts $6.8 billion full-year profit
stories.why_it_matters: Westpac reported a full-year profit of $6.8 billion, a solid result that underscores just how much the banks are benefiting from higher interest rates — even as borrowers struggle. It's a reminder of the two-speed economy: big institutions are thriving while households are squeezed. The result is likely to renew political pressure on the banks to pass on rate cuts more quickly when the cycle eventually turns.

stories.title: Matt Canavan to run in Capricornia for One Nation
stories.why_it_matters: Former LNP senator Matt Canavan has confirmed he will run for the seat of Capricornia under the One Nation banner, after One Nation's James Ashby ruled out a tilt at the seat. Canavan, a vocal resources sector advocate and critic of the net-zero agenda, jumping to One Nation signals a further fracturing of the conservative side of politics. It could complicate the Coalition's vote in Queensland resource communities and is worth watching as the federal political landscape shifts.

stories.title: Gina Rinehart blasts government's net-zero agenda as Hancock profits drop
stories.why_it_matters: Mining billionaire Gina Rinehart hit out at the federal government's net-zero emissions agenda after Hancock Prospecting reported a drop in profit. Rinehart, who pays one of Australia's largest individual tax bills, argued that green energy policies are hurting Australian industry competitiveness. The comments come as the resources sector faces a double-whammy of weaker commodity prices and increasing regulatory pressure — a tension that directly affects stocks like Pilbara Minerals and the broader resources sector.

stories.title: Albanese to discuss rule change for British backpackers
stories.why_it_matters: PM Albanese is set to discuss potential changes to working holiday visa rules for British backpackers — likely extending the time they can work in Australia or easing restrictions on where they can work. Australia has a genuine labour shortage in regional areas, and British backpackers are a key part of the seasonal workforce. Any changes would help address gaps in agriculture, hospitality, and tourism — sectors that have been stretched since the pandemic.

ai.summary: Google continues its multi-front AI push with a new security-focused model, pricing competition is intensifying across the major AI platforms, and the US midterms are putting AI regulation firmly in the spotlight.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon — an AI built specifically to find and fix security flaws
stories.why_it_matters: Google has released Gemini 4 Carbon, a specialised AI model designed to automatically detect and fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities in software. This is a big deal for businesses — instead of paying expensive security consultants to manually audit code, companies could soon use AI to scan and patch weaknesses continuously. It's another sign that AI is moving from general-purpose chat tools to highly specialised professional applications.

stories.title: Gemini 3.1 Pro priced aggressively against Claude and GPT — the AI price war heats up
stories.why_it_matters: Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro is being priced at $2/$12 per million tokens (input/output) — aggressively undercutting competitors like Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT models. This pricing battle is great news for businesses using AI tools, as costs keep coming down. For investors in GOOG, it signals Google is fighting hard for market share in the AI API space — important given the Search revenue concerns flagged elsewhere today.

stories.title: Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic pledge new controls on AI data scraping
stories.why_it_matters: The three biggest AI labs — Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic — have jointly pledged new controls on how their AI systems scrape and use data from the web. This is partly a response to mounting legal pressure from publishers and creators who argue their content is being used without permission or payment. For everyday users, it could mean AI tools start being more transparent about where their answers come from — and for media companies, it could eventually mean licensing deals or revenue sharing with AI firms.

stories.title: US midterms put AI regulation in the spotlight — divided Congress likely means gridlock
stories.why_it_matters: Financial institutions are watching the US midterms partly through the lens of AI regulation — if Democrats sweep Congress, stronger AI oversight laws become more likely. Major banks see limited immediate market impact from a divided government scenario, but longer term, the regulatory environment for AI companies like Google and Microsoft could shift significantly. Congress is already scrambling to keep pace with how fast AI is developing, and the election outcome will shape who gets to write the rules.

stories.title: AI image generation showdown: blind tests crown a clear winner in 2026
stories.why_it_matters: A blind test pitting ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, and Claude against each other for image generation has apparently crowned a clear winner in 2026 — though the article doesn't reveal which in the headline. What it signals is that the AI image space has become genuinely competitive, with each platform now capable of producing high-quality visuals. For everyday users, this means better creative tools across the board — and for AI-exposed investors, it's a reminder that competition is fierce and no single player has a permanent lead.

sport.summary: The Roosters clinched the NRL Grand Final over the Knights in a thriller, 19-18. Off the field, Addo-Carr's drugs saga takes a new twist, the NRL transfer period kicks off with 176 players in free agency, and there's big news around Nathan Cleary and the PNG NRL team.

stories.title: Roosters win the NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights in a classic
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have won the 2026 NRL premiership, beating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a nail-biting Grand Final at Accor Stadium. One point was the margin — it doesn't get closer than that. For Roosters fans, it's another title to add to the famous tri-colours' collection. Knights fans will be heartbroken, having come agonisingly close to their first premiership in decades.

stories.title: Addo-Carr drugs saga: second test result lands before crunch Eels meeting
stories.why_it_matters: The result of Josh Addo-Carr's second drugs test has come back just before a critical meeting with Parramatta Eels officials that could determine his future at the club. The Fox Sports report describes it as a 'huge twist' — suggesting the result may not be what was expected. Addo-Carr has been one of the most explosive players in the game, so his availability (or lack thereof) is a major storyline heading into the off-season.

stories.title: 176 NRL players enter free agency as transfer period opens
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL's off-season transfer window has officially opened with 176 players now in free agency — meaning clubs can move quickly to sign talent for next season. This is the busiest time of year for player movements and contract dramas. The Sydney Chiefs are among the clubs looking to splash cash, reportedly chasing a marquee halfback with tax-free incentives. Expect big signing announcements over the coming weeks.

stories.title: Nathan Cleary call stuns as PNG signs $900k star
stories.why_it_matters: There's a stunning development involving Nathan Cleary — the details aren't fully clear from the headline alone, but News.com.au describes it as a call that 'stuns.' Separately, Papua New Guinea's NRL expansion team has signed a $900,000 star — a significant investment that signals the PNG team is building seriously for their entry into the competition. The expansion of NRL into PNG is one of the biggest growth stories in rugby league history.

stories.title: Broncos coach Madge delivers 'new start' message after rough 2026 season
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire (Madge) has addressed fans after what sounds like a difficult 2026 season, promising a fresh start and reset heading into pre-season. The Broncos are one of the NRL's most high-profile clubs, and after the Roosters' Grand Final victory, attention will quickly turn to which clubs can challenge in 2027. Madge's message suggests significant changes are coming at Red Hill.
